=== FORMAL LETTER OF OPPOSITION - 59142_57_1682331 - McCabe 11.18.26.pdf ===
BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS

PROJECT NO. 59142

REVIEW OF ERCOT'S INTERCONNECTION PROCESSES FOR LARGE LOADS

PUBLIC COMMENT IN OPPOSITION TO SYNERGEN GREEN ENERGY, INC.'S REQUEST
FOR GOOD CAUSE EXCEPTION

To the Commissioners of the Public Utility Commission of Texas:

I am submitting this public comment in strong opposition to Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s
September 11, 2026 filing requesting a good cause exception to ERCOT's Batch Zero
eligibility deadlines.

I respectfully urge the Commission to DENY Synergen's request.

I am a concerned citizen with an interest in the long-term welfare of Calhoun County, Texas.
I am not seeking to intervene as a party in this proceeding. I am submitting these comments
so that the concerns of affected residents are included in the Commission's consideration
of this request.

This is not simply a matter of whether a private company would prefer additional time to
qualify for an electricity interconnection study. It is a matter of whether established
regulatory requirements will be applied consistently, whether a private developer will be
granted relief after failing to meet applicable requirements, and whether the public interest
will be given appropriate weight.

1. Established Deadlines and Regulatory Requirements Must Mean Something

ERCOT established a published implementation schedule for Batch Zero. That schedule
included a readiness kickoff, release of documentation, submission deadlines, and project
classification milestones.

The published timeline identified:

   •   May 15, 2026 — Batch Zero readiness kickoff.

   •   Early June 2026 — Release of implementation documentation.

   •   July 10, 2026 — Deadline for applicable large-load project submissions.

   •   July 24, 2026 — Deadline for applicable transmission and distribution provider
       eligibility materials.
    •   August 7 and August 31, 2026 — Original project classification and final inclusion
       milestones.

These dates demonstrate that Batch Zero was implemented through an organized process
with identified milestones. The Commission should not disregard those requirements simply
because a developer now faces financial or scheduling consequences.

If Synergen failed to satisfy applicable requirements by the established deadlines, it should
be required to demonstrate specific, compelling, and documented circumstances
establishing why an exception is justified.

A developer's desire to preserve its investment, avoid delay, or maintain its preferred
construction schedule is not, standing alone, sufficient justification for regulatory relief.

A deadline is not meaningful if a company can miss it and then rely on the financial
consequences of its own delay to obtain an exception.

Granting this request without a compelling, independently supported explanation would
raise serious questions about equal treatment and the integrity of the Batch Zero process.

2. Synergen's Financial Investment Does Not Establish Good Cause

Synergen places considerable emphasis on its claimed $30.5 million investment and the
financial consequences it may face if its project is delayed.

Those investments were made as part of a private business venture. They do not create an
entitlement to an exception, nor should they shift the consequences of a developer's failure
to meet regulatory requirements onto the public or other electricity customers.

Every developer pursuing a major industrial project is responsible for understanding
applicable requirements, planning accordingly, and meeting established deadlines.

The Commission should not allow the size of a company's investment or the amount of
money it stands to lose to determine whether regulatory requirements will be enforced.

Regulatory standards must apply equally, regardless of a developer's financial
resources, political support, or projected economic impact.

3. The Proposed Facility's Electricity Demand Deserves Serious Scrutiny

Synergen's proposed ammonia facility represents an exceptionally large electricity demand
for a rural area.

The project materials describe electricity requirements and capacity on the scale of
approximately 300 MW. A demand of this magnitude cannot be treated as an ordinary
 industrial connection or approved without a clear understanding of its implications for the
regional electric grid.

Before granting any exception that advances this project through the interconnection
process, the Commission should have reliable information addressing:

   •   The facility's actual anticipated electricity consumption, not simply its proposed
       capacity.

   •   Its normal operating demand and maximum peak demand.

   •   Its expected load profile and the likelihood of continuous, around-the-clock
       operation.

   •   Whether and how the facility can reduce consumption during periods of grid stress.

   •   The transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure necessary to serve the
       facility.

   •   The estimated cost of those improvements and who will be responsible for paying
       them.

   •   Whether any costs could ultimately be passed on to existing electricity customers.

   •   The potential effect on regional grid reliability during periods of high demand or
       limited generation.

The public should not be expected to accept general assurances that a project will not
negatively affect the grid. These questions require technical documentation and an
independent assessment.

The Commission should not grant an exception first and leave fundamental questions
about the project's electricity requirements and grid impacts unanswered.

4. Renewable Energy Contracts Are Not the Same as Dependable Electricity Supply

Synergen represents that its project will have access to approximately 890 MW of renewable
generation, consisting of 290 MW of solar generation and 600 MW of wind generation through
a virtual power purchase agreement.

These claims require careful examination.

A virtual power purchase agreement does not, by itself, establish that electricity generated
by a particular wind or solar facility will be physically delivered to Synergen's facility at the
time it needs power.
 Solar generation is dependent on daylight and weather conditions. Wind generation is
variable. Neither source, by itself, guarantees continuous electricity supply.

The Commission should require documentation establishing:

   •   Whether the proposed generation facilities are operational, under construction, or
       merely planned.

   •   Whether the stated generation capacity is committed and contractually secured.

   •   Whether the electricity will be physically deliverable to the project or whether the
       agreements are financial arrangements.

   •   How the facility will obtain electricity when wind and solar generation are insufficient.

   •   Whether supplemental electricity will be drawn from the ERCOT grid.

   •   How the project will operate during periods of limited renewable generation or grid
       stress.

The existence of renewable energy contracts should not be treated as proof that a 300
MW industrial load will not place substantial demands on the Texas electric grid.

The Commission should evaluate the project's actual electrical requirements and its
dependence on grid-supplied power, rather than relying on renewable-energy claims alone.

5. Projected Economic Benefits Do Not Override Regulatory Responsibilities

Synergen promotes approximately 60 permanent jobs, 150 construction jobs at peak, and
substantial projected project expenditures and regional economic benefits.

These figures are projections, not guaranteed outcomes.

Temporary construction employment is not the same as permanent employment. Projected
economic activity is not the same as money actually delivered to local governments,
schools, and taxpayers.

The Commission should not allow projected jobs, tax revenue, or economic impact to
substitute for compliance with established interconnection requirements.

Nor should the Commission assume that the economic benefits will necessarily outweigh
the costs associated with major transmission improvements, electricity demand, and other
infrastructure requirements.

Calhoun County's future should not be placed at risk based solely on a developer's
economic projections.
 A private company's projected economic benefits do not give it the right to bypass
established regulatory requirements.

6. The Concerns of Affected Communities Should Not Be Dismissed

Synergen's representatives have emphasized the project's anticipated economic benefits
and have solicited letters of support. However, support for economic development should
not be confused with unanimous community support for this particular project.

Calhoun County residents have legitimate concerns about the scale and long-term
consequences of the proposed facility.

Those concerns include electricity demand, water resources, environmental impacts, air
quality, wastewater, industrial safety, and the future character of our communities.

I am not opposed to responsible industrial development. I am opposed to the assumption
that a large private development should receive special consideration simply because its
representatives promise jobs and economic growth.

Residents should not be characterized as obstacles to progress because they ask
reasonable questions about a project that could have long-term consequences for their
community.

The Commission's responsibility is to evaluate the regulatory request before it—not to
decide whether residents should support Synergen's business plan.

7. An Electricity Interconnection Exception Must Not Be Confused With Project
Approval

I recognize that many concerns involving water use, air quality, wastewater, environmental
protection, and industrial safety fall under the jurisdiction of other regulatory agencies.

However, granting Synergen a good cause exception should not be portrayed as evidence
that these matters have been resolved or that the facility has received all required permits
and approvals.

An exception allowing a project to proceed through an interconnection study process is not
the same as approval to construct or operate the facility.

The Commission should make clear that any decision in this proceeding does not prejudge
or replace other required regulatory reviews, permits, or approvals.

The fact that a project may qualify for further electricity studies does not establish that it is
environmentally acceptable, economically justified, or in the best interests of the affected
community.
 8. The Commission Should Deny the Request and Protect the Integrity of the Process

The purpose of established interconnection requirements is to provide a consistent,
transparent, and fair process for evaluating large electricity loads.

Granting exceptions without a compelling and documented basis risks undermining that
process. It also raises the possibility that other developers will expect similar treatment
when they fail to satisfy established requirements.

Synergen's investment, construction schedule, projected employment, and potential
financial losses do not eliminate its responsibility to comply with applicable requirements.

The Commission should not create a precedent in which a developer's financial exposure
becomes a substitute for good cause.

If Synergen believes the requirements were unfair, unclear, or impossible to meet, it should
be required to substantiate those claims with specific evidence. General complaints about
the new process or the financial burden of compliance are not enough.

REQUEST FOR COMMISSION ACTION

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Public Utility Commission of Texas:

   1. DENY Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s request for a good cause exception.

   2. Require Synergen to demonstrate specific, documented, and compelling grounds for
      any requested relief from applicable Batch Zero requirements.

   3. Decline to treat the company's private financial investment, projected economic
      benefits, or potential construction delays as sufficient justification for an exception.

   4. Preserve the integrity and consistent application of ERCOT's established
      interconnection requirements.

   5. Require adequate technical support for the project's anticipated electricity demand,
      renewable generation claims, and potential impact on regional grid reliability before
      relying on those claims in evaluating the request.

   6. Ensure that project-related transmission and infrastructure costs are properly
      identified and allocated, without unfairly burdening existing electricity customers.

   7. Make clear that any interconnection determination does not constitute approval of
      the facility or replace any other required state, federal, or local permits and regulatory
      reviews.
 CONCLUSION

Calhoun County residents deserve consideration when decisions involving projects of this
magnitude are being made.

The proposed Synergen facility represents a significant industrial development with
substantial electricity requirements and potential long-term implications for the
surrounding region.

This Commission has an obligation to uphold the regulatory process and ensure that
established requirements are not treated as optional when compliance becomes
inconvenient for a private developer.

Synergen's investment is its business decision. Its projected jobs and economic benefits are
its projections. Its responsibility to satisfy applicable regulatory requirements remains its
own.

The people of Texas should not be asked to accept weakened regulatory standards
simply because a private company has invested money and now wants an exception.

Economic development is important, but it must be pursued responsibly, transparently, and
under the same rules that apply to everyone.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Commission to DENY Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s
request for a good cause exception.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Respectfully submitted,



Michelle McCabe
Calhoun County, Texas
11/18/2026
